title: Yet You Did Not Return to Me
summary: Amos calls the wealthy women of Samaria "cows of Bashan" who oppress the poor and demand drinks from their husbands, and he warns that they will be dragged out through broken walls. He mocks the busy worship at Bethel and Gilgal. God then lists the warnings he has already sent (famine, drought, blight, locusts, plague, war, and overthrow), each ending with the refrain "yet you did not return to Me", and he calls Israel to prepare to meet its God, the creator of mountains and wind.
story: Chapter 3 announced that God would punish his chosen people and destroy the altars and houses of Samaria and Bethel. Chapter 4 fills in the picture from three angles: the luxury of Samaria's elite, the hollow religion of the northern shrines, and a history of warnings ignored. The refrain of verses 6 to 11 shows that judgment is not God's first word but his last, after years of patient calls to return. The chapter's closing summons, "prepare to meet your God", leads into the lament and the call to "Seek the LORD and live" in chapter 5.
historical:
Samaria in the time of Jeroboam II (about 793 to 753 BC) was home to a wealthy class whose comfort depended on the produce and labor of the countryside. Inscribed potsherds found at Samaria, known as the Samaria ostraca and usually dated to the first half of the eighth century BC, record shipments of wine and oil from surrounding estates to officials in the capital, illustrating the flow of goods into the city that Amos saw. The women addressed in verse 1 belonged to this privileged circle.

The disasters in verses 6 to 11 cannot be tied to particular years, but drought, crop disease, locusts, epidemic, and military defeat were all familiar in Israel's recent memory; Israel had suffered badly in wars with Aram in the late ninth century (2 Kings 13:7). Harmon, the destination of the exiled women in verse 3, is unknown; the word may be a place name or a scribal form of another name, and translations vary. The exile itself came when Assyria deported much of the northern population after 722 BC.
cultural:
Bashan, the fertile plateau east of the Sea of Galilee, was famous for its rich pastures and its well-fed cattle (Deuteronomy 32:14; Psalm 22:12; Ezekiel 39:18). Calling the women of Samaria "cows of Bashan" pictured them as sleek, pampered, and heavy with good living. The hooks of verse 2 may reflect the way captives were led away, sometimes by ropes or hooks through the nose or lip, as Assyrian reliefs depict prisoners; other interpreters think the images come from fishing or from butchers' hooks.

Verses 4 and 5 are a parody of a priest's invitation to worship: "Go to Bethel and transgress". Bethel and Gilgal were major pilgrimage sanctuaries. The law called for tithes annually and a special tithe every third year (Deuteronomy 14:22-29); Amos's "every three days" exaggerates the worshipers' zeal to expose it. Thank offerings could include leavened bread (Leviticus 7:13), but freewill offerings were meant to be voluntary and quiet, not advertised. The disasters listed in verses 6 to 11 closely follow the covenant curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28, the warnings Israel had accepted at Sinai. "Cleanness of teeth" is a vivid idiom for famine: there is nothing to chew.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1 to 3 address the women of Samaria with an oath: God swears by his holiness. Verses 4 and 5 are ironic, a call to worship that is really a call to sin. Verses 6 to 13 are a carefully built poem of five (or, counting the sword and plague together, seven) disasters, each closing with the same line, "yet you did not return to Me", declares the LORD. The repetition has the force of a sad drumbeat. Verse 12 is left open ("that is what I will do to you") without naming the punishment, which makes it more ominous, and it ends with the summons to prepare to meet God. Verse 13 is the first of three hymn-like passages in Amos (see also 5:8-9 and 9:5-6) praising God as creator; some scholars think these doxologies were added later, while others see them as Amos's own use of familiar hymns.

outline.t: The cows of Bashan led away with hooks
Warnings sent, yet you did not return
Prepare to meet your God, the creator

doctrines.note: The refrain "yet you did not return to Me" shows that God's warnings were meant to bring his people back. Repentance was always the goal; judgment comes only after repeated invitations are refused.

God swears "by His holiness" in verse 2. His holiness, his absolute moral purity and otherness, stands behind his judgment of oppression and empty worship. What God swears by his own nature, he will do.

Verse 13 names God as the one who forms the mountains and creates the wind. The creator of the whole world is the one Israel must meet, which means there is nowhere to hide from him and no power greater than his.

words.note: Parah, cow or heifer. Amos's use for the women of Samaria is a deliberate shock, drawn from the language of the herdsman he was. The image points to well-fed comfort bought at the expense of the poor they "oppress" and "crush".

Shuv, to return or turn back. It is the key to the refrain in verses 6 to 11. Every disaster was meant as a summons to turn around and come back to God. The word will be central to the prophets' call to repentance, and Hosea ends his book with it (Hosea 14:1).

Kun, to establish or prepare. "Prepare to meet your God" echoes the instructions at Sinai, when Israel was told to be ready for the third day because the LORD would come down (Exodus 19:11-17). The meeting that once meant covenant now means judgment.

Bara, to create, the verb of Genesis 1:1, which in this form always has God as its subject. In verse 13 God "creates the wind". The doxology reminds Israel that the God it has ignored is not a local deity but the maker of everything.

christ: The chapter's refrain describes a God who sends warning after warning because he wants his people back. Jesus embodied that same persistence when he lamented over Jerusalem: "how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling" (Matthew 23:37). The summons to "prepare to meet your God" takes on a new shape in the New Testament, where people meet God in the person of Jesus and are called to be ready for his return (Matthew 24:44). The creator praised in verse 13, the one who reveals his thoughts to man, is the God who, according to John and Paul, made all things through his Son (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16). These connections are thematic rather than predictive.

hard.q: Is it demeaning for Amos to call women "cows of Bashan"?
hard.a: The insult is sharp, and it is meant to be. Several things put it in context. Bashan's cattle were proverbial for their quality and fatness, so the image was about pampered comfort rather than ugliness. The women are condemned not for being women but for their conduct: they "oppress the poor and crush the needy" and push their husbands for more luxury. Amos's rhetoric is equally hard on men throughout the book (the judges who take bribes, the merchants who cheat, the rich lounging on ivory beds), and elsewhere the prophets speak with similar bluntness about the powerful of both sexes (Isaiah 3:16-26 on the women of Jerusalem, Isaiah 5:11-12 on the men). Some interpreters also think the phrase may have been drawn from religious language associated with Bashan, though that is uncertain. Readers may still feel the harshness, and that is part of Amos's purpose: he uses shocking language to break through the complacency of people who did not see the cost of their comfort to others.

questions: The women of Samaria enjoyed comforts that others paid for. What comforts in your own life might depend on someone else's hardship?
The refrain "yet you did not return to Me" recurs five times. What warnings or wake-up calls have you been slow to heed?
Israel's worship was busy and generous but did not lead to justice. How can you tell whether worship is drawing you toward God or merely making you feel religious?
